End-to-End Differentiable Simulator Design

Vision

Transform Powerful.jl from a power flow solver into a differentiable simulation engine that enables:

  • Gradient-based controller optimization
  • Parameter learning from data
  • Sensitivity analysis for planning
  • Co-design of physical systems and control

Reverse-Mode AD: What It Is

Both forward-mode and reverse-mode autodiff are mathematically exact - they compute derivatives to machine precision. The difference is computational cost:

Forward-Mode (what you have now)

  • Cost: O(n_inputs) evaluations to compute full Jacobian
  • Good for: Many outputs, few inputs (Jacobians in power flow: ∂g/∂y)
  • Example: 135,800 variables → Jacobian with 135,800 columns
    • With sparsity coloring: Only 34 forward passes!

Reverse-Mode (for optimization)

  • Cost: O(n_outputs) evaluations to compute full gradient
  • Good for: One output, many inputs (gradients of scalar objectives: ∂loss/∂p)
  • Example: Scalar cost function → gradient w.r.t. 1,000 parameters
    • Reverse-mode: 1 backward pass vs 1,000 forward passes

Power Systems Applications

Reverse-mode enables:

  1. Optimal Power Flow (OPF): Minimize generation cost subject to constraints
  2. Controller Tuning: Optimize PI/PID/droop gains for stability
  3. Parameter Estimation: Fit inertia, impedance from PMU measurements
  4. Planning: Sensitivity of voltage stability margin to network upgrades

User Experience Design

Typical Simulation User (No Changes Needed)

# Load case
case = PowerFlowData.parse_network("ieee14.raw")

# Build models with normal Float64 parameters
pq = parse_model(PQ, case)  # PQ loads with fixed P, Q values
pv = parse_model(PV, case)  # Generators with fixed Pg, Vset
branch = parse_model(Branch, case)  # Lines with fixed impedances

# Create system and solve - same as always
sys = SystemModel(AddressManager(), (; Bus=bus, PQ=pq, PV=pv, Branch=branch))
solve_power_flow(sys)

No overhead, no complexity, works exactly as before.

Advanced Optimization User (Opt-In Complexity)

using Powerful, Optimization, OptimizationOptimJL, ComponentArrays

# Step 1: Identify what parameters you want to optimize
# Use ComponentArray for named, hierarchical parameter structure
p = ComponentArray(
    droop_R = fill(0.05, 10),      # Frequency droop coefficients
    pg_ref = fill(1.0, 10),         # Generator setpoints
    avr_gains = (kp=fill(20.0, 10), ki=fill(5.0, 10))  # Voltage regulator gains
)

# Step 2: Create system builder that uses these parameters
function build_system_with_params(p, base_case)
    # Parse base case
    pq = parse_model(PQ, base_case)
    pv = parse_model(PV, base_case)
    branch = parse_model(Branch, base_case)

    # Override specific parameters you want to optimize
    # (Keep types generic to support Dual numbers)
    pv.pg_ref .= p.pg_ref
    pv.droop_R .= p.droop_R
    pv.avr_kp .= p.avr_gains.kp
    pv.avr_ki .= p.avr_gains.ki

    return SystemModel(AddressManager(), (; Bus=bus, PQ=pq, PV=pv, Branch=branch))
end

# Step 3: Define objective function
function objective(p, base_case, measurements)
    # Rebuild system with current parameters
    sys = build_system_with_params(p, base_case)

    # Solve power flow (will be made differentiable)
    y = solve_power_flow(sys)

    # Compute loss
    v = get_bus_voltages(sys, y)
    voltage_dev = sum((v .- 1.0).^2)          # Minimize voltage deviation
    control_penalty = 0.01 * sum(p.pg_ref.^2) # Minimize generation

    return voltage_dev + control_penalty
end

# Step 4: Optimize with automatic differentiation
prob = OptimizationProblem(
    (p, _) -> objective(p, base_case, measurements),
    p;  # Initial parameter guess
    grad = true  # Enable AD for gradients
)

sol = solve(prob, BFGS())

println("Optimal parameters: ", sol.u)

Key insight: The complexity is isolated to optimization users. Regular users never see it.

Ergonomic Design Principles

Principle 1: Separation of Concerns

Models are generic, but construction is typed:

# Model definition (in src/models/pv.jl)
@kwdef struct PV{Tv}  # Generic over Tv (voltage type), NOT parameter type
    pg_ref::Vector{<:Number}  # Can be Float64, Dual, or tracked types
    droop_R::Vector{<:Number}
    # ... other fields
end

# Residual functions already handle generic arrays correctly
function calc_residuals!(
    ws::ResidualWorkspace{T, AT},
    model::StructArray{<:PV}  # NOT PV{T} - you already fixed this!
) where {T, AT}
    # Works for any element type in model arrays
end

User never specifies types explicitly:

# Normal use - concrete types
pv = PV(pg_ref = [1.0, 2.0], droop_R = [0.05, 0.05], ...)

# Optimization use - let Julia infer types from p
pv = PV(pg_ref = p.pg_ref, droop_R = p.droop_R, ...)
# If p contains Dual numbers, arrays will be Vector{Dual}
# If p contains Float64, arrays will be Vector{Float64}

Principle 2: Explicit Parameter Mutation

Problem: Which model fields are "parameters" vs "state" vs "structure"?

Solution: User explicitly updates what they want to optimize.

# Helper function approach
function set_generation_setpoints!(sys::SystemModel, pg_ref::AbstractVector)
    sys.models.PV.pg_ref .= pg_ref
    return nothing
end

function set_droop_coefficients!(sys::SystemModel, R::AbstractVector)
    sys.models.PV.droop_R .= R
    return nothing
end

# In objective function
function objective(p, sys_template)
    sys = deepcopy(sys_template)  # Or create fresh system
    set_generation_setpoints!(sys, p.pg_ref)
    set_droop_coefficients!(sys, p.droop_R)

    y = solve_power_flow(sys)
    return compute_loss(y, ...)
end

Alternatively, use closure pattern:

# Create parameterized system builder
function make_parameterized_system(base_case)
    # Parse base topology/structure once
    base_models = parse_all_models(base_case)

    # Return builder function
    function build(p)
        # Shallow copy models
        models = copy(base_models)

        # Update optimizable parameters
        models.PV.pg_ref .= p.pg_ref
        models.PV.droop_R .= p.droop_R

        return SystemModel(AddressManager(), models)
    end

    return build
end

# Usage
build_sys = make_parameterized_system(case)

function objective(p, _)
    sys = build_sys(p)  # Fast: only updates parameters
    y = solve_power_flow(sys)
    return compute_loss(y, ...)
end

Principle 3: Type Stability Through Reconstruction

Challenge: Switching between Float64 and Dual numbers breaks type stability.

Solution: Rebuild system for each parameter type (overhead is acceptable for optimization).

# This pattern preserves type stability
function objective(p::ComponentArray{T}, base_case) where T
    # System will be type-stable: SystemModel{T, ...}
    sys = build_system_with_params(p, base_case)

    # Solver will be type-stable
    y = solve_power_flow(sys)  # Returns Vector{T}

    return compute_loss(y)::T  # Returns scalar of type T
end

# ForwardDiff or Zygote will call this with p::Vector{Dual{...}}
# Julia compiles specialized version for Dual types
# Overhead: One-time compilation, amortized over optimization iterations

Implementation Architecture

Phase 1: Enable Generic Parameters (Minimal Changes)

Goal: Make sure parameter fields can hold Dual numbers without breaking.

Checklist:

  1. Check model field types:

    # ❌ Don't constrain to Float64
@kwdef struct PQ{Tv}
    pg::Vector{Float64}  # BAD
    qg::Vector{Float64}  # BAD
end

# ✅ Use abstract types or unconstrained
@kwdef struct PQ{Tv}
    pg::Vector{<:Number}  # GOOD
    qg::Vector{<:Number}  # GOOD
end

  2. Test with ForwardDiff:

    using ForwardDiff, Test

@testitem "PQ model supports Dual numbers" begin
    # Create PQ with Dual parameters
    pg_dual = [ForwardDiff.Dual(1.0, 1.0), ForwardDiff.Dual(2.0, 0.0)]
    qg_dual = [ForwardDiff.Dual(0.5, 0.0), ForwardDiff.Dual(0.3, 1.0)]

    pq = PQ(pg=pg_dual, qg=qg_dual, ...)

    # Should not error
    @test eltype(pq.pg) <: ForwardDiff.Dual
end

  3. Ensure residual functions are generic:

    # Should already work - you use ResidualWorkspace{T} pattern
function calc_residuals!(
    ws::ResidualWorkspace{T, AT},
    model::StructArray{<:PQ}
) where {T, AT}
    # T will be Dual when computing derivatives
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(model)
        ws.res_vals.p[i] = model.pg[i] * ws.var_vals.v[i] + ...
        # Works for any T<:Number
    end
end

Phase 2: Implicit Differentiation (Performance)

Goal: Make solve_power_flow differentiable via implicit function theorem.

Math: Power flow satisfies g(y, p) = 0

By implicit differentiation:

dy/dp = -(∂g/∂y)^(-1) * (∂g/∂p)
       = -J^(-1) * B

Where:

  • J = ∂g/∂y is the Jacobian (you compute this already!)
  • B = ∂g/∂p is residual sensitivity to parameters

Implementation: Create src/powercore/implicit_diff.jl

using ChainRulesCore, SparseArrays, LinearAlgebra

"""
    compute_parameter_jacobian(sys::SystemModel, y, p_indices) -> B

Compute ∂g/∂p for specific parameters.

# Arguments
- `sys`: System model
- `y`: Current state (solution)
- `p_indices`: Which model fields are parameters (specified by user)

# Returns
- `B::SparseMatrix`: Residual sensitivity to parameters
"""
function compute_parameter_jacobian(sys::SystemModel, y, param_info)
    # This is model-specific - each model needs to declare parameter dependencies
    # For now, use forward-mode AD to compute B columns

    n_res = length(sys.dae.g)
    n_params = total_num_params(param_info)

    B = spzeros(n_res, n_params)

    # For each parameter, perturb and compute ∂g/∂pᵢ
    # (Can be parallelized, vectorized with SparseDiffTools later)

    param_idx = 1
    for (model_name, field_name, indices) in param_info
        model = getfield(sys.models, model_name)
        field = getfield(model, field_name)

        for i in indices
            # Perturb parameter with dual number
            orig_val = field[i]
            field[i] = ForwardDiff.Dual(orig_val, 1.0)

            # Compute residuals
            ws = ResidualWorkspace(sys, ForwardDiff.Dual{Float64})
            update_workspace!(ws, sys.dae, y)  # Load state
            compute_all_residuals!(ws, sys.models)

            # Extract dual parts
            g_dual = ws.res_vals  # Named tuple of residuals
            B[:, param_idx] = extract_derivatives(g_dual)

            # Restore
            field[i] = orig_val
            param_idx += 1
        end
    end

    return B
end
"""
    rrule for solve_power_flow

Enables reverse-mode AD through implicit differentiation.
"""
function ChainRulesCore.rrule(
    ::typeof(solve_power_flow),
    sys::SystemModel,
    param_info  # User-specified: which parameters to differentiate
)
    # Forward solve
    y = solve_power_flow(sys)

    function pullback(ȳ)
        # ȳ = ∂loss/∂y (upstream gradient from loss function)

        # Compute Jacobian J = ∂g/∂y at solution
        cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(sys)
        sparsity = jacobian_sparsity_pattern(sys)
        colors = matrix_colors(sparsity)
        J = Float64.(sparsity)
        forwarddiff_color_jacobian!(J, cache, y; colorvec=colors)

        # Solve adjoint equation: J^T λ = ȳ
        # Reuse sparse factorization from forward solve!
        λ = J' \ ȳ

        # Compute parameter sensitivity B = ∂g/∂p
        B = compute_parameter_jacobian(sys, y, param_info)

        # Chain rule: ∂loss/∂p = -λ^T * B
        p̄ = -λ' * B

        return NoTangent(), NoTangent(), p̄
    end

    return y, pullback
end

Usage:

using Zygote

# Define which parameters to differentiate
param_info = [
    (:PV, :pg_ref, 1:10),   # All 10 generators' setpoints
    (:PV, :droop_R, 1:10),  # All 10 droop coefficients
]

# Now solve_power_flow is differentiable!
loss(p) = begin
    # Update system parameters
    sys.models.PV.pg_ref .= p[1:10]
    sys.models.PV.droop_R .= p[11:20]

    # Solve (differentiable via ChainRules)
    y = solve_power_flow(sys, param_info)

    # Compute loss
    return compute_loss(y)
end

# Get gradient
dp = Zygote.gradient(loss, p)

Phase 3: User-Friendly API

Goal: Hide complexity behind nice interface.

Create src/solvers/optimization.jl:

using ComponentArrays, ChainRulesCore

"""
    ParameterMap

Maps ComponentArray parameter vector to system model fields.

# Example

julia pmap = ParameterMap( :PV => [:pgref, :droopR], # PV model fields :AVR => [:kp, :ki] # AVR model fields )

"""
struct ParameterMap
    mappings::Dict{Symbol, Vector{Symbol}}
end

"""
    update_system_parameters!(sys, p, pmap::ParameterMap)

Update system model fields from parameter vector.
"""
function update_system_parameters!(sys::SystemModel, p::ComponentArray, pmap::ParameterMap)
    for (model_name, fields) in pmap.mappings
        model = getfield(sys.models, model_name)

        for field in fields
            if haskey(p, field)
                getfield(model, field) .= getfield(p, field)
            end
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

"""
    differentiable_solve(sys::SystemModel, p::ComponentArray, pmap::ParameterMap)

Solve power flow with differentiable parameters.

Returns state vector `y` with ChainRules support for reverse-mode AD.
"""
function differentiable_solve(sys::SystemModel, p::ComponentArray, pmap::ParameterMap)
    # Update parameters
    update_system_parameters!(sys, p, pmap)

    # Solve with custom rrule
    y = solve_power_flow(sys, pmap)

    return y
end

Performance Characteristics

Implicit Differentiation (Recommended Approach)

For ACTIVSg 70k system (135,800 variables, 1,000 parameters):

OperationTimeNotes
Forward solve (Jacobian)~140msUsing SparseDiffTools colored Jacobian
Adjoint solve (J^T λ = ȳ)~140msReuse Jacobian sparsity pattern
Parameter Jacobian (∂g/∂p)~1000ms1,000 forward-mode perturbations
Total gradient~1.3sOne complete ∂loss/∂p

Compare to:

  • Finite differences: 1,000 × 140ms = 140 seconds (100x slower!)
  • Forward-mode only: 1,000 × 140ms = 140 seconds (100x slower!)

Why Reverse-Mode Wins

If you have:

  • n = 135,800 state variables (y)
  • m = 1,000 parameters (p)
  • Scalar loss function

Forward-mode cost: O(m) = 1,000 evaluations to get full ∂loss/∂p Reverse-mode cost: O(1) = 1 backward pass to get full ∂loss/∂p

Challenges and Solutions

Challenge 1: Discontinuities in Power Systems

Problem: Hard limits, tap changers, topology switching.

Solutions:

  1. Smooth approximations:

    # Instead of hard clamp:
pg = clamp(pg_desired, pg_min, pg_max)  # Not differentiable at boundaries!

# Use smooth penalty:
function smooth_clamp(x, xmin, xmax; k=100)
    # Softplus-based smooth approximation
    x_low = xmin + softplus(k*(x - xmin))/k
    x_clamped = xmax - softplus(k*(x_low - xmax))/k
    return x_clamped
end

  2. Penalty methods:

    # Add barrier to objective
barrier = sum(relu(pg - pg_max).^2 + relu(pg_min - pg).^2)
loss = physics_loss + 1e6 * barrier

  3. Sub-gradients: For piecewise-linear functions, use sub-differential.

Challenge 2: Non-Convergent Solutions

Problem: Power flow may not converge for some parameter values during optimization.

Solutions:

  1. Large penalty:

    function safe_solve(sys)
    try
        y, converged = solve_power_flow(sys; maxiter=20, tol=1e-6)
        if !converged
            return nothing
        end
        return y
    catch
        return nothing
    end
end

function objective(p, sys)
    y = safe_solve(sys)
    if isnothing(y)
        return 1e10  # Large penalty
    end
    return compute_loss(y)
end

  2. Constrained optimization: Add feasibility constraints.

  3. Trust region: Limit parameter step size.

Challenge 3: Computational Cost

Problem: Rebuilding system for each parameter update might be expensive.

Solution - Parameter View Pattern:

"""
    ParameterizedSystem

Wraps system with mutable parameter vector.
No rebuilding needed - just update reference.
"""
struct ParameterizedSystem{T}
    sys::SystemModel{T}
    p::ComponentArray{T}  # Shared reference
    pmap::ParameterMap

    function ParameterizedSystem(sys, p, pmap)
        # Point model fields directly to p slices
        update_system_parameters!(sys, p, pmap)
        new{eltype(p)}(sys, p, pmap)
    end
end

# When p changes, sys.models.PV.pg_ref automatically sees new values (shared reference)
# No rebuild needed!

Example Applications

Application 1: Frequency Droop Tuning

Goal: Optimize droop gains for frequency regulation after generator trip.

function frequency_regulation_objective(droop_gains, base_case, disturbance)
    # Build system with these droop gains
    sys = build_system_with_params((droop_R=droop_gains,), base_case)

    # Simulate disturbance (lose one generator)
    trajectory = simulate_disturbance(sys, disturbance, tspan=(0.0, 10.0))

    # Penalize frequency deviation
    freq_error = trajectory.freq .- 60.0  # Hz
    max_deviation = maximum(abs.(freq_error))
    settling_time = compute_settling_time(freq_error, threshold=0.1)

    # Multi-objective
    return max_deviation + 0.1 * settling_time
end

# Optimize
droop_opt = optimize(frequency_regulation_objective, droop_initial)

Application 2: Estimating Generator Inertia from PMU Data

Goal: Fit inertia constants H to measured frequency response.

function pmu_fitting_loss(inertia, pmu_data, event)
    # Update generator inertia
    sys = build_system((H=inertia,), base_case)

    # Simulate same event PMU recorded
    sim_freq = simulate_event(sys, event, pmu_data.tspan)

    # Least squares error
    error = sim_freq .- pmu_data.measured_freq
    return sum(error.^2)
end

# Fit
H_fitted = optimize(pmu_fitting_loss, H_initial)

Application 3: Co-Optimizing Battery Placement and Droop

Goal: Decide where to place batteries AND how to set droop gains.

function codesign_objective(design, scenarios)
    # design.battery_sizes: where to place (continuous: MVA per bus)
    # design.droop_gains: how to control

    total_cost = 0.0

    for scenario in scenarios
        sys = build_system_with_batteries(design.battery_sizes, design.droop_gains)

        # Run power flow
        y = solve_power_flow(sys, scenario.loads)

        # Compute cost
        losses = compute_losses(sys, y)
        voltage_quality = sum((get_voltages(sys, y) .- 1.0).^2)

        total_cost += losses + 10.0 * voltage_quality
    end

    # Add capital cost
    total_cost += sum(design.battery_sizes) * battery_cost_per_mva

    return total_cost / length(scenarios)
end

# Optimize
design_opt = optimize(codesign_objective, design_initial)

Testing Strategy

Test 1: Forward-Mode Through Models

@testitem "Models support ForwardDiff" begin
    using ForwardDiff

    # Create PQ with dual-valued parameters
    pg = ForwardDiff.Dual.(fill(1.0, 5), fill(1.0, 5))
    pq = PQ(pg=pg, qg=zeros(5), ...)

    @test eltype(pq.pg) <: ForwardDiff.Dual
end

Test 2: Implicit Diff vs Finite Differences

@testitem "Implicit differentiation matches finite differences" begin
    using FiniteDiff

    # Setup
    sys = create_test_system()
    p = [1.0, 2.0]  # Two parameters

    # Objective
    f(p) = begin
        update_params!(sys, p)
        y = solve_power_flow(sys)
        return sum(y.^2)  # Dummy loss
    end

    # Finite differences
    grad_fd = FiniteDiff.finite_difference_gradient(f, p)

    # Implicit differentiation
    grad_impl = Zygote.gradient(f, p)[1]

    @test norm(grad_fd - grad_impl) < 1e-6
end

Test 3: Optimization Convergence

@testitem "Parameter optimization converges" begin
    # Simple optimization problem
    sys = create_test_system()

    # True parameters
    p_true = [0.05, 1.0]

    # Noisy measurements
    y_measured = solve_power_flow(sys, p_true) + 0.01 * randn(n)

    # Fit
    loss(p) = sum((solve_power_flow(sys, p) - y_measured).^2)

    p_initial = [0.1, 0.5]
    p_opt = optimize(loss, p_initial)

    @test norm(p_opt - p_true) < 0.01  # Should recover true parameters
end

Summary

What Reverse-Mode Gives You

  • Efficient gradients for optimization: O(1) instead of O(m) cost
  • Enables applications: OPF, controller tuning, parameter estimation
  • NOT about accuracy: Both forward and reverse are exact

Ergonomic Design

  1. Default users: No changes, no overhead - use as normal
  2. Optimization users: Explicit parameter mapping with ComponentArrays
  3. Type stability: Rebuild system for each parameter type (acceptable cost)

Architecture

  1. Phase 1: Verify models support generic parameter types (may already work!)
  2. Phase 2: Implement implicit differentiation via ChainRules
  3. Phase 3: Build user-friendly ParameterMap API

Key Implementation Insight

Your Jacobian infrastructure (∂g/∂y) is 90% of what you need for implicit differentiation. Just add parameter sensitivity (∂g/∂p) and wire up ChainRules.
